speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: It's integrated into a modern open fan architecture that together will be sustainable aviation fuel ready. It will be hydrogen capable and it will have more than 20% fuel burn advantage over today's engine with all of these technologies together. And we'll test that and do a fly demo on that also by the middle of this decade.
finding: Commits RISE to a 20%+ fuel-burn target and a flight demonstration by mid-decade.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: Many in the industry said there is no way GE Aviation will certify a plastic fan blade. We failed twice. We got it done because we have the conviction and the grid and because the laws of physics says it can be done.
finding: Shows high technology risk appetite: persisting through failures on composite fan blades on conviction grounded in physics.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: We have done what we always do here, which there was an issue. It was in testing here in-house. And we understood the issue, understand the root cause, provided the right inspection and fixes, which was satisfying for the Boeing team and for the FAA.
finding: Handles the GE9X issue that paused 777X flight testing with a root-cause, inspect-and-fix routine agreed with Boeing and the FAA.
trigger: 777X test fleet grounded for a GE9X issue

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: Some of the fixes would provide lift to everybody, we're going to go provide it to everybody. Some of the fixes are only intended and they provide only the time-on-wing improvements for the Middle East, those will go. And we are debating, "Do we give it to everybody?" Because that also gives flexibility of moving the fleet.
finding: Decides fix rollout through a formal configuration board, weighing targeted versus fleet-wide fitment.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: GE90 has a stable, reliable architecture. And we only needed to change a handful of parts ... And let me tell you, anybody who will tell you that they need to redesign a large portion of the engine in order to achieve the customer expectations, you should be worried.
finding: Contrasts LEAP's 'handful of parts' fixes with rivals needing major redesigns, an implied jab at the GTF.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: LEAP, the fleet leader, is achieving 10,000 cycles, precisely 9,882 cycles ... CFM56 in the same environment roughly achieves in the neighborhood of 17,000 cycles ... Today, LEAP fleet leaders achieve about 4,800 and some cycles, close to 5,000 cycles. That's compared to CFM56 achieving in a similar environment somewhere in the neighborhood of 7,000 to 8,000 cycles.
finding: Discloses the LEAP durability gap to CFM56 with field data in both benign and harsh environments rather than hiding it.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: last year, we stood in front of you, and we told you we'll introduce the fuel nozzle coking fix in 2024. And I'm proud to stand here in front of you and say that the first production engine with that fix is already at Airbus ready to go.
finding: Checks back publicly against last year's dated commitment and reports it met: the LEAP-1A fuel-nozzle fix is in production.
trigger: June 2023 commitment to certify the fuel-nozzle coking fix by end-2023 and introduce it in 2024
response: first production engine with fix delivered to Airbus by March 2024

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: we expect production engines at the end of this year to be at the mature time on wing for LEAP-1A, and 1B will follow in 2025 ... it's not on the back of a theory. It's not on the back of analysis. And certainly, it's not on the back of wishful thinking. It's because we have done real testing.
finding: Makes a dated durability commitment and grounds his confidence in physical test evidence, not analysis.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: This is what we call turn on and turn off. Turn on the problem in an actual condition and turn it off in testing with the new design. And to be honest with you, if it's not turn on and turn off, I will not believe the outcomes, and this is why we feel confident.
finding: His evidence standard for a fix: reproduce the field failure in test, then show the redesign removes it ('turn on, turn off').

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: We find problems before problems find us because when they find us, they are painful and expensive. And that's why we have institutionalized enhanced inspection of our safety critical parts in all of our new make shops and in our MRO network as well.
finding: Signature engineering rule: hunt for defects proactively, built into inspection everywhere, because problems found late are costly.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: it's practically impossible to achieve that 20% fuel burn improvement without the open fan. And the reason is physics ... a ducted engine, which is one that has a nacelle around it, has less than half the fuel burn improvements that can come from an open fan.
finding: Argues on physics for the CFM RISE open fan over ducted next-generation designs; ducted engines would get less than half the gain.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: we have learned and institutionalized that no single person can make a safety decision. No single person can make a safety decision. It's always a teamwork. It's always a cross-functional team making the safety calls.
finding: Sets decision rights: safety calls are never made by one person, only by cross-functional teams.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: And on the CFM RISE program, we're working with our partner, Safran, and we are at a stage of program in which we are making real testing ... we have tested also noise working with Airbus, and we have showed and demonstrated that the open fan technology has the capability to achieve lower noise than today's LEAP.
finding: Runs RISE as a joint CFM/Safran programme and de-risks it with an airframer partner (Airbus noise testing).

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: In the case of Power Generation Services, it is a high-margin, high-return business that requires significant technology and manufacturing supply chain investment. We believe this is a business that should generate about 20% margins and returns over 20% over time.
finding: Sets explicit margin and return targets by business model; installed-base services businesses (like Aviation services) are held to about 20% margins and over 20% returns.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: what we've laid out here is we expect a 15-plus percent IRR. And we expect to hurdle our weighted average cost of capital by 2018.
finding: Applies a two-part acquisition test: an IRR of 15% or more and returns above the cost of capital within about three years.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We see the deal IRR of at least 15-plus percent in our base plan, and we still believe we can deliver $0.15 to $0.20 of earnings in 2018.
finding: Commits to a return and EPS contribution for the Alstom deal; by late 2017 Power, Alstom's core, was GE's main problem.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We're basically telling you if we run the place the way we just closed it and deliver all of the cost synergies, we ... generate very attractive returns.
finding: Underwrites deals on cost synergies only, treating growth synergies as upside.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: in our incentive compensation plan that we completely restructured beginning this year, delivering on these synergies will be a significant piece of that construct for each one of these businesses and for the company in its totality.
finding: Ties business leaders' incentive pay to deal-synergy delivery to enforce accountability.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: From a capital allocation perspective, I mean, the returns on the restructure we've done has been phenomenal. The execution within the businesses and delivering the paybacks, and that's part of the reason you've seen the margin expansion
finding: Treats restructuring as a high-return use of capital and credits it for margin expansion.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: I think we feel very good about the guidance we gave you in December around the outlook for Alstom in 2016 of $0.05 contribution. That, today, feels very solid. And I'd go back to what we said about 2015 on that call. We came in almost line item by line item virtually right on top of what we told you.
finding: Backs a new commitment by pointing to having met the previous one line by line.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: And the only decrement, if you will, as you describe it, is we are overcoming the launch costs and the launch margins associated with the LEAP and the H, the wind turbines, et cetera, et cetera. So we will grow op profit next year.
finding: Commits to 2016 profit growth despite LEAP launch margins; GE delivered 2016 EPS of $1.49 within its range.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We shipped 59 GEnx units versus 77 last year, driven by schedule. We have no delinquencies to Boeing.
finding: Volunteers on-time delivery status to the airframer customer, treating airframer delinquency as a key operating metric.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: For the year, revenues grew 3%, operating profit grew 11% and margins expanded 160 basis points. Our share on each of our engine platforms is very strong, and the LEAP launch remains on track for midyear.
finding: Enters the LEAP launch year with Aviation margins expanding and the launch on schedule.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: And when you look at orders in the quarter, particularly in Power, orders price has been very, very good, very strong, particularly on the H turbine, largely because we're selling out slots.
finding: Raises price when delivery slots are scarce, using sold-out capacity as pricing power.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We need our big Service businesses, PGS and Aviation, to grow and deliver what they -- because we have these product launches. So we've got the H turbine coming next year. We've got a little over 100 LEAP engines launching next year.
finding: Relies on Aviation and Power services growth to fund the margin dilution from the LEAP and H-turbine launches.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Portfolio quality remained stable, and the Aviation portfolio finished the quarter with 0 delinquencies and only 2 AOGs.
finding: Monitors aircraft-leasing (GECAS) credit through airline delinquencies and grounded aircraft, the main aviation balance-sheet exposure.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We have a big backlog in Aviation associated with the Emirates, Qatar airlines, et cetera. I don't think in the case of Power or Aviation that we have concerns about our Middle East backlog in any way, shape or form.
finding: Treats Gulf carrier engine backlog as firm despite regional risk.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: the differences in exchange between the U.S. and China are pretty de minimis. A lot of our business, like Aviation, are dollar based.
finding: Views Aviation as largely insulated from currency risk because engines and services are priced in dollars.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: That is built on those investments that we made in the toughest part of the cycle that massively differentiated us coming out of the cycle. That's what we need to do with Oil & Gas.
finding: Keeps R&D rising in a downturn while cutting structural cost, applying the Aviation lesson across the portfolio.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We'll ship the first roughly 100 LEAP engines that power the 737 and the A320. Midyear, we'll start shipping those engines. We're extraordinarily excited about it. As you know, we've got an enormous backlog. The engine has been hugely commercially successful.
finding: Sets an initial 2016 LEAP delivery target of about 100 and highlights the backlog; actual 2016 deliveries were 77.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: So what it allows us to do is make those kinds of maintenance and work scope decisions on an engine, a serial number, based on its behavior, not on fleet averages, and that's enormously valuable.
finding: Sees engine-by-engine data ('digital twin') as the way to run aftermarket work scopes and time on wing, increasing services profitability.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: So a lot of new technology entering the portfolio, and it's critical that these launches happen on time, on cost and on performance.
finding: Treats on-time, on-cost, on-spec execution of 2016 launches (LEAP, H turbine, Tier 4) as a top priority.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: But that price point for us has got to be a price point that leaves enough margin that we can generate a return on capital that's attractive to those that own the company. And so I think cost is every bit as strategically important to competitiveness as having the newest whiz-bang technology
finding: Ranks product cost equal to technology as a competitive weapon, tied to earning an attractive return on capital at a market price point.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: What the -- what our teams and our businesses need to be focused on are being hypercompetitive, winning every single opportunity when the opportunity presents itself. At times, creating demand where demand is not naturally happening
finding: Sets a win-every-campaign priority, including using GE financing to create demand.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: And as you know, in our company, from a profitability perspective, it's all about the installed base, and it's all about services. So winning these deals early is critically important to how we think about the profitability of the company down the road. And the more competitive and the higher win rate, the more we'll make in the future.
finding: States the installed-base logic that drives aggressive original-equipment pricing: win the placement now, earn on services later.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: So we actually for our jet engine or our gas turbine, we create a Digital Twin of the actual operating asset and we collect all the data we can -- we know everything about that asset. It's almost like a P&L of 1.
finding: Treats each installed engine as its own profit unit, the logic behind long-term service agreements.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: When the world settles on a platform solution, and whatever the space, mobile telephony, pick your space, search, the world settles on 2 or 3 solutions. That's it. You could show up a year later with the world's greatest version. It doesn't matter. The world's made its decision.
finding: Believes platform markets lock in two or three winners early, so being first to scale matters more than being best later, the same logic as engine programme positions.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Everybody hated the industry. They hated our jet engine business, and that is exactly when we doubled our investment in what today is the LEAP engine, the GE9X engine, et cetera, and that's what -- today, we have, I don't know, 75%, 78% share in large commercial engine. That's not by accident.
finding: Cites GE Aviation's counter-cyclical R&D bet in the early-2000s downturn (which produced LEAP and GE9X) as the model for investing through a downturn.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: What we're not going to do is a deal where we're underwriting oil being at $50 12 months from now to make it all look -- that doesn't make any sense.
finding: Will not do an acquisition whose case depends on an optimistic market recovery; requires deals to work on a pragmatic market view.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: So I think your teams have to be focused on winning and executing flawlessly to the things they do control. In other words, it really doesn't help, Jeff and I, when the team comes in to tell us that oil is down below $30. I read the paper, too.
finding: Holds business leaders accountable for controllables (winning deals, cost) rather than accepting macro explanations.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: I think the margin rate in the second quarter, based on LEAP, both launch and initial shipments, and H, we'll get better sequentially every quarter on H costs. I think margin rate will be a little bit of a challenge in the second quarter. No change on how we think about it for the year.
finding: Pre-warns of near-term margin pressure from the LEAP launch while holding the full-year commitment.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The LEAP launch remains on track, and we expect to ship 15 to 20 units in the second quarter and about 110 engines for the year. We've now accumulated more than 19,000 cycles on the LEAP engine, and all the engines were performing well and all were meeting their fuel specifications.
finding: Gives quarterly and annual LEAP delivery targets at launch; the second quarter delivered 11 and the year 77.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: we're, despite that, through all the investment we've made around restructuring, SG&A costs, the focus on supply chain, that we're going to overcome those costs and grow margins roughly 50 basis points in the year ex Alstom.
finding: Commits to grow margins about 50 bps in 2016 despite new-product launch costs (LEAP, H turbine, wind) by offsetting them with structural cost-out.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Operating profit in the quarter was higher by 16% on Services volume and cost productivity, and operating profit margins expanded 110 basis points. Aviation had another solid quarter.
finding: Aviation's profit growth in the pre-LEAP quarter rests on services volume and productivity.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We expect to get deeper down the curve on the LEAP engine as volume ramps in 2017 versus 2016
finding: Plans LEAP economics on a learning curve: unit cost falls as volume ramps, so early losses are expected to narrow.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: On the ride there, we have a very attractive dividend yield. We're at least 100 basis points in excess of the average of the S&P 500.
finding: Treats the dividend yield premium to the S&P 500 as a core investor proposition.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: No change to the framework for the year, $1.45, $1.55 of earnings. We still think we're on track for 2% to 4% organic growth here for the year.
finding: Holds the 2016 EPS framework mid-year despite a second-half-loaded plan; the year closed at $1.49, inside the range.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: we expect organically to grow our profit between 2016 to 2018, about 5%. And so, which puts us on the path to be plus $2 a share when we get out to 2018.
finding: Commits to a $2-plus 2018 EPS target in June 2016; by mid-2017 he was guiding 2017 to the bottom of its range and by October 2017 the cash plan had collapsed, so the target was not reaffirmed in the slice.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Where is it that there's a technology or capability that we think is critically important we own? That -- and we own it either by organically developing it or maybe by buying it. But then we clearly -- it's not something we want to partner, it's not something we want to share, et cetera.
finding: Separates capabilities GE must own outright from those it will partner on, and treats critical technology as not for sharing.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Another axis to consider is time. So this is absolutely a race against the clock, in our view.
finding: Uses speed to market as a reason to buy capability rather than build it over 12-18 months.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: sometimes the analytic insights you get from Predix in this capability, your solution set may be to actually physically change the asset itself, a different coding, a different tolerance, et cetera. Those are things we can only do within our own installed base.
finding: Sees the OEM's ability to redesign its own installed base as an edge in the services business that third parties cannot match.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: the more successful we are around changing outcomes, the more differentiation you have around our products, not just our service products, not just our software products, but our original equipment products. And, so the theory of the case, whether you decide to exploit that in terms of share or whether you try to exploit it with a better price
finding: Treats product differentiation as a choice between taking share or taking price.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: This makes a ton of sense for the company as we already own the excess debt and the borrowing cost is lower than our dividend yield. The proceeds were used for an accelerated share repurchase program launched in June.
finding: Uses a simple test for debt-funded buybacks: borrow when the borrowing cost is below the dividend yield.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: While we plan to be down in the first half, we underperformed our own expectations by roughly $1 billion, driven by lower collections, accelerated inventory build and earlier closing of appliances transaction in the quarter than we had originally planned. Fortunately, most of this is timing
finding: Calls a first-half cash miss 'timing' and holds the full-year framework, a pattern repeated in 2017; the 2016 range was later narrowed to $11-12 billion.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The Aviation team continues to execute well, and as mentioned, we shipped our first 11 LEAP engines and are scheduled to ship about 110 for the year.
finding: Sets a 2016 LEAP delivery target of about 110 in July; it fell to about 105 in October and 77 actual.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Operating profit was higher by 6%, driven by services volume, positive value gap and cost productivity. Margins in the quarter expanded 40 basis points.
finding: Attributes Aviation's profit growth to services volume and pricing over cost inflation ('value gap') as LEAP-1A deliveries begin.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: This quarter, we booked $1.4 billion of commercial engine orders, including Aviajet order for 200 LEAP 1B engines. In addition, we took orders for 348 CFM engines, 21 CF6 engines and 29 GEnx engines.
finding: Reports LEAP-1B and CFM56 order flow together, with legacy CFM56 still taking volume during the transition.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: I think the $3 billion to $5 billion are cost-out goals. Obviously, an enormous motivation for making this investment in this set of technology. I think most of that value creation is going to happen outside of the 2018 window.
finding: Accepts a long payback on the additive manufacturing acquisitions (Arcam, SLM), justified by product-cost savings mainly after 2018.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: the standard doesn't just impact aircraft engine. It will impact all of our business to varying degrees. We're in the very early stages of going through what that might look like, et cetera.
finding: Refuses to quantify an accounting change affecting aircraft-engine profit until the work is done, and insists it does not change the economics.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: This gain was partially offset by a charge associated with the anticipated sale of our majority share in a nonstrategic business in aviation that makes aerial structures.
finding: Prunes non-core Aviation businesses (aerostructures) to focus Aviation on engines and services.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: And certainly, with the stock at $28 to $29, the buyback looks quite attractive to us. We're not short ideas on M&A, I don't think.
finding: Makes buyback intensity price-sensitive, leaning into repurchases when the share price is low while keeping M&A capacity.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Industrial CFOA is expected to generate between $11 billion and $12 billion of cash for the total year.
finding: Narrows 2016 cash guidance in October; actual came in at $11.6 billion, inside the range.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We have shipped 33 LEAP engines to date, and there are currently 6 LEAP-powered planes flying with 2 airlines, with departure performance of 100%, and some of those planes operating more than 10 cycles a day. We expect to deliver about 105 engines this year.
finding: Forecasts about 105 LEAP deliveries for 2016 in October; the year closed at 77, which he later attributed to coordination with the airframers.
lag: missed by 28 engines within one quarter

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Operating profit of $1.5 billion was up 10%, driven by higher volume and cost productivity. Margin rates improved 120 basis points in the quarter.
finding: Aviation delivers margin expansion during the early LEAP ramp through volume and productivity.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: In the quarter, we booked $1.4 billion of new engine orders, including about $400 million in LEAP, $250 million of CFM and $350 million of GEnx.
finding: Tracks CFM56 and LEAP orders side by side as the narrowbody transition proceeds.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We believe the combination will be accretive to GE shareholders beginning in 2018, and is consistent with our framework of underwriting transactions that achieve returns of 15% or better.
finding: States GE's M&A hurdle explicitly: underwrite acquisitions to a 15%-or-better return.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: So we've tried to take what I would describe as a reasonably pragmatic approach on how we thought about the recovery.
finding: Underwrites a cyclical acquisition on assumptions well below consensus (Baker EBITDA at 60% of the 2014 peak by 2020).

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: we obviously underwrote it downside case as well, where you -- essentially, oil does nothing for the next 3 or 4 years. And even in that case, largely driven by the synergy value that's created here, we're better off as a company having done the deal than not doing the deal.
finding: Requires a deal to still create value in a flat-market downside case, relying on synergies rather than market recovery.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: That's not always on the GE Capital balance sheet. As a matter of fact, we'd like to -- as much as possible, we'd like them to use other syndicate debt, syndicate equity and use other people's capital to make these deals happen.
finding: Prefers customer financing that uses third-party capital rather than GE's balance sheet, while still using finance to win orders.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: No, we're not putting more capital into GE Capital, I can assure you of that. I don't want anybody to walk away to think we're running behind plan, we're running ahead of plan.
finding: Gives a categorical assurance on GE Capital capital needs, emphasising being ahead of plan.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: I want to be clear that the tax benefits associated with the disposition did not fall through to our earnings. They were spent in restructuring charges.
finding: Pre-empts low-quality-earnings criticism by stating that a tax-driven gain on a non-core Aviation exit was offset by restructuring.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The gain was not recorded in Aviation, okay? That was recorded at corporate. It was offset in restructuring. So none of the gain results are reflected in the segment performance at Aviation.
finding: Defends the quality of Aviation's reported segment earnings by isolating one-off gains at corporate.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We had expected to ship a total of about 100 engines in 2016 but, in coordination with the airframers, we delivered 77 for the total year, meeting all our commercial commitments. These units will now deliver in 2017 with total shipments of about 500 LEAP engines for next year.
finding: Explains a LEAP first-year shortfall (77 vs about 100) as agreed with the airframers and rolls the units into a roughly 500-engine 2017 target.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Our expectation is the spares sales rate, the ADOR, will not be up that strongly next year. We're thinking high single digits.
finding: Guides Aviation spares growth down from double digits to high single digits for 2017, rather than extrapolating a strong year.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: we're going to continue to grow the operating profit in Aviation next year, notwithstanding the LEAP shipments. So right now, our estimate is we'll ship something close to $500 million -- 500 -- 500 LEAP engines next year, and that's factored into that outlook.
finding: Commits to Aviation profit growth in 2017 with the 500-engine LEAP ramp already baked into the plan.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The business shipped its first LEAP engines. And currently, 20 A320neos powered by LEAP are flying across 6 different customers. Reliability has been excellent, and the engines are performing to spec.
finding: Reports LEAP-1A entry into service on the A320neo with reliability claims and no hedging.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: A lot of that being renegotiated terms. We've talked about realigning or aligning suppliers with customers in terms of the time sync between build and collect.
finding: Uses supplier payment-term renegotiation to match supplier payments with customer collections, a cash lever that shifts burden onto the supply chain.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Op profit in the quarter totaled $1.7 billion, up 11%, primarily driven by favorable price, volume and productivity, partly offset by the LEAP mix. Margins expanded 100 basis points in the quarter.
finding: Shows Aviation can expand margins while absorbing the start of negative-margin LEAP deliveries.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: we took a lot of headwind this year on the H launch, both the ramp of the H and the individual unit cost. Now the units we shipped in the second half of the year were profitable, significantly more profitable than the beginning of the year, but still much less profitable than a lot of the F technology
finding: Accepts first-year margin dilution on a new product launch, expecting a learning curve and pricing to recover it, the same logic applied to LEAP.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: every day that those businesses are part of portfolio, you could argue we're actually destroying value, not creating value. They can't compete for capital. They're not a core focus. And in some of these, you need to be a buyer, and if you're not a buyer, you need to be a seller.
finding: States a portfolio rule: if a business cannot compete for capital and GE will not be a buyer in its industry, sell it.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We met all the goals and all the underwriting targets that we gave investors when we initially announced the Alstom deal. We over-delivered on synergies. We accelerated a lot of restructuring to get those synergies.
finding: Claims the Alstom acquisition met its underwriting case; later in 2017 Power, Alstom's core, became the main source of GE's miss.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: If we do that and we deliver on the profitability, 100 basis points of margin improvement both in '17 and '18, we should deliver free cash flow conversion that looks like something like 95%, the way we've been measuring.
finding: Commits to 100 bps of margin improvement per year and about 95% free cash flow conversion; 2017 industrial cash ended near a $7 billion construct against a $12-14 billion plan.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Well, we were -- EPS is up double digits in '16. We expect to be up double digits in '17, and we expect to be double digits in '18.
finding: Gives a multi-year double-digit EPS growth commitment in February 2017; by July he was guiding 2017 to the bottom of the $1.60-1.70 range and by October cash guidance had fallen to about $7 billion.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: So it has crystallized the focus inside the company around cost as it should, and we just need to create more buffer and how we think about cost, given where some of these businesses are in their cycle
finding: Responds to margin slippage by building cost buffers into plans so commitments survive cyclical downturns.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Everybody is getting paid on cash, the focus is enormous. I have more than 100 resources to incorporate idle staff, some consultants and others and the corporate team that are working every day with the individual businesses on inventory payables, receivables, work-in-progress.
finding: Runs cash as a centrally driven programme with incentive pay tied to cash and a corporate team embedded in the businesses.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The other's in our long-term service contract accounting, and we have an enormous portfolio, many times bigger than anybody else in space, both in power -- principally in power system and aviation.
finding: Sees the scale of GE's long-term service contract book in Aviation and Power as a competitive differentiator.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: A big part of this analytic capability is the service contract. We've been a lot smarter about how we think about executing against those contracts and the cost to do it.
finding: Links digital analytics directly to lower cost of executing service contracts, the profit engine in Aviation.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: There will be no margin smoothing over the life of the contract, which means that, in general, like on the LEAP engine, where those will ship at losses, they'll ship with their actual loss. And when we ship a spare engine, that would be wildly profitable
finding: Spells out CFM engine economics: LEAP install engines are sold at a loss and spare engines are highly profitable; new accounting will show both.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: when we talked in April 2015, we talked about a business that we thought could return 10% or 11%, okay? I think we're still kind of in that ballpark. I think, the GE Cap -- the Commercial Aviation business is a good -- very good business with very good returns.
finding: Holds GE Capital to a roughly 10% return target and singles out aircraft leasing (GECAS) as the strong-return piece.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Going forward, our spares rate will only include externally shipped spares and spares used in time and material shop visits.
finding: Changes the headline Aviation spares metric to exclude LTSA-consumed spares, re-defining a KPI investors track and justifying it as better market visibility.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We expect to see most of this come back over the remainder of the year, and we see no change for our outlook for the year of $12 billion to $14 billion of industrial CFOA.
finding: Reaffirms the cash range after a $1 billion first-quarter miss; it later fell to the bottom end (July) and about $7 billion (October).

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The business is generating strong productivity to offset the negative mix impact of LEAP and is on track to report 2017 margin rates about flat with last year on continuing cost improvements. We will continue to ramp production to an expected 450 to 500 LEAP shipments for the year.
finding: Commits to flat Aviation margins through the LEAP ramp and to 450-500 LEAP deliveries in 2017.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We're not pulling future profit forward. That is not what we're doing. We're just restating what -- where we are in the contract from inception to date.
finding: Rebuts the charge that service-contract margin updates inflate earnings, insisting they reflect real cost improvements.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: In Aviation, which historically has not had issues with past dues, we missed by about $200 million on 5 customer accounts, which will clear in the second quarter with no issue.
finding: Treats an Aviation collections slip as timing and commits to its recovery the next quarter.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The other $800 million are contract adjustments driven by better cost performance and part life, primarily driven by Power and Aviation.
finding: Explains service-contract accounting: better part life on Aviation and Power contracts raises booked margin before cash arrives.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Op profit in the quarter totaled $1.7 billion, up 10%, primarily driven by favorable price, volume and cost productivity, partly offset by a negative impact of 81 LEAP shipments versus 0 last year.
finding: Treats each LEAP shipment as a margin drag to be absorbed by price and productivity elsewhere in Aviation.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The second part is where the long-term service agreements that protect our installed base, our penetration continues to improve. When you look at the attach rate on the H turbine, on the LEAP engine, the population and our backlog around this contracts is growing substantially
finding: Values new engine programmes like LEAP by the long-term service agreements attached to them, which protect the installed base.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: And then there's a small update for escalation that's mostly around our Aviation business. We update it once a year on escalation within the service contract.
finding: Describes annual price escalation built into Aviation long-term service contracts, a contractual price lever on the installed base.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: I think what you get with John is a deep intellectual curiosity, a willingness to challenge the status quo, completely objective view about what the right thing to do with the next $1 of shareholder money.
finding: Describes the incoming CEO-CFO partnership in capital-allocation terms: objective, marginal-dollar decisions.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: John and I were doing our capital allocation plan for the year. Dividend remains our priority. We are relooking the $11 billion to $13 million range on cash used for buyback based on the timing of dispositions.
finding: Ranks the dividend above buybacks and makes buyback size contingent on disposal proceeds.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: I think our share buyback has always been predicated on dividends from GE Capital and the disposition. So I -- no change in there.
finding: States the buyback is funded from GE Capital dividends and disposal proceeds, not industrial free cash flow.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: if there are capital market solutions to help customers do that and we're pricing for that as opposed to us essentially pricing it, I'm wide open on that. Those structures are not simple.
finding: Open to moving the financing of long-term service upgrades to capital markets when the customer pays for it, but only for fixed payments.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: At the Paris Air Show, we announced $31 billion in orders and commitments, including new engine commitments totaling $21 billion and services of $10 billion. None of these announcements were booked into orders in the second quarter.
finding: Separates air-show announcements from booked orders, signalling a conservative order-recognition policy.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We've got some really big deals in the second half that could put 20 or 30 of those units at risk. I'm not telling you the business doesn't think they're going to deliver them. I'm just highlighting for you there could be a risk there.
finding: Flags downside risk while keeping the business's number intact; the 155-165 AGP target was later cut to 80-90.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The last thing I'd tell you, just because -- in the quarter, nobody asked, but our CMRs or LTSAs in the quarter were $500 million. They were $600 million in the second quarter of last year.
finding: Volunteers the long-term service agreement catch-up figure unprompted, pre-empting criticism of LTSA accounting.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: For the year, we are trending to the bottom end of the $12 billion to $14 billion range on CFOA, driven by pressure principally at Power and Oil & Gas.
finding: Moves the cash guide to the bottom of range in July rather than cutting it; by October the construct was about $7 billion.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The LEAP engine continues to perform to spec, with 62 aircraft flying today. The business is on track to ship 450 to 500 LEAP engines this year.
finding: Gives a dated LEAP delivery commitment for 2017 and vouches for field performance.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: As LEAP shipments accelerate in the second half, we expect the margins to be pressured and still expect total year margin rate to be roughly flat with 2016.
finding: Pre-warns that the LEAP second-half ramp will pressure margins while holding a flat full-year Aviation margin commitment.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Operating profit of $1.5 billion was up 11%, primarily driven by higher service volume and base cost productivity, which more than offset the negative LEAP margin.
finding: Describes the LEAP ramp as negative-margin original equipment funded by aftermarket services, the core economics of the CFM model.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: 70 million of LDs were really around 3 large H unit, where we took a little bit of risk on schedule and commissioning not having been through the process. And it took us a bit longer to get there.
finding: Acknowledges that committing to schedules on a new product introduction carried liquidated-damages risk that materialised.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: I think John wants to go back and rethink about how we think about capital allocation in the company and embedded in that, obviously, is how we think about share buyback.
finding: Defers capital-allocation decisions to the incoming CEO's review, showing the CFO aligning to the new CEO's decision rights.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: As you know, we're in the process of performing an actuarial analysis of claims reserves in our insurance business. Until that review has been completed, we have deferred the decision to pay GE Capital dividends to GE.
finding: Holds back upstream cash (GE Capital dividends of about $3 billion) until a reserve review is finished rather than distributing on a provisional basis.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: there is no mismatch of receivables or timing between GE and GE Capital, whatsoever. And we don't have any reason to believe that the $155 billion of assets that GE Capital has is not going to service their outstanding debt.
finding: Answers a balance-sheet concern with a flat, categorical denial ('whatsoever').

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: we had a $500 million correction for the first half related to derivative-hedged settlements that had been incorrectly classified in operating cash flow versus investing cash flow. Our first half CFOA was underreported by $500 million.
finding: Discloses a cash-flow classification error openly on the call, quantifying it rather than burying it in filings.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The new guidance we have for the total year includes an outlook for Power in the fourth quarter that should derisk our volume assumptions. We are now forecasting AGPs at 80 to 90 for the total year, down from the previous 155 to 165 forecast.
finding: Resets a volume forecast he had reaffirmed in April and July by roughly half, and describes the new number as 'derisked'.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: So where we were overoptimistic planning on both services and units inventory, that inventory is going to liquidate over time.
finding: Admits over-optimistic planning drove an inventory build of almost $2 billion, while arguing it will turn to cash.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: I've talked a lot about accountability inside the company, and that sense of accountability has to start with me. We are not living up to our own standards or those of investors, and the buck stops with me.
finding: Owns the 2017 operating and cash miss personally and frames his exit as CFO as an act of accountability rather than blaming the businesses.
response: steps down as CFO, hands role to Jamie Miller

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We are severely disappointed in the results of Power and are taking action to position the business going forward. This includes a refocus on the basics; significant additional cost-out plans; and changes to management
finding: Responds to a collapsing business with a standard playbook: back to basics, cost-out and replacing leaders.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: We don't have a cost structure that reflects the market that it's competing in, and we need to get at it.
finding: Diagnoses the problem as structural cost mismatched to market size and makes cost resizing the first lever.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: one of the things we're trying to do is get the business stabilized on what is a pragmatic look at volume, ... not just in the fourth quarter but for 2018, that sets the business up for the long term.
finding: After a miss, shifts planning toward conservative ('pragmatic') volume assumptions rather than stretch targets built on short-cycle conversion.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: The business shipped 111 LEAP engines, including 23 Boeing 1B retrofitted engines associated with the LPT disc issue from earlier in the year.
finding: Reports LEAP ramp volumes with the LEAP-1B low-pressure-turbine disc retrofit called out, keeping a quality escape visible in the shipment count.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: Operating profit in the quarter of $1.7 billion was up 12%, primarily driven by volume, structural cost productivity and value gap, partially offset by margin pressure from higher LEAP shipments.
finding: Frames Aviation profit as services/cost-driven with the LEAP ramp as a known, accepted margin headwind.

speaker: Jeffrey S. Bornstein, Former Vice Chair
quote: GECAS annual impairments totaled about $50 million, primarily driven by 4 777 aircraft.
finding: Reports aircraft-leasing impairments tied to older widebody types, showing GE's residual-value exposure on the fleet it finances.

speaker: William A. Fitzgerald, Vice President and General Manager of Commercial Engines Operation
quote: Suppliers have a role in that. We're going to enable them to have jobs for 30 years. They ought to help us get this thing down the cost curve.
finding: Would not give a LEAP OE breakeven year in 2017 ('I wouldn't count on which year'); expects suppliers to fund cost-down in return for 30-year programme volume.

speaker: William A. Fitzgerald, Vice President and General Manager of Commercial Engines Operation
quote: Look, we want to run this system 6 to 8 months ahead of what the rate demand is really going to be at that time." So we've been running our supply chain at higher rates, literally, 2 quarters out.
finding: Accepted working-capital cost to run the LEAP supply chain two quarters ahead of demand and find bottlenecks early.

speaker: Gautam J. Khanna, Cowen and Company, LLC, Research Division
quote: Right. I guess, one of the things that makes it a little bit more complex is the other partner on the LEAP engine, Safran. And they have some sole-source positions with suppliers.
finding: The ramp risk lies partly in Safran's half of the LEAP supply chain, which GE does not control directly.

speaker: William A. Fitzgerald, Vice President and General Manager of Commercial Engines Operation
quote: And Safran is a terrific partner. In fact, their entire supply chain and our entire supply chain are down in Auburn, Alabama, at one of our new sites, studying once again where could the pinchpoints be, right.
finding: Ramp readiness is done jointly: the two parents review each other's supply chains together.

speaker: William A. Fitzgerald, Vice President and General Manager of Commercial Engines Operation
quote: And I -- candidly, I probably talk to my counterpart 3 or 4 days a week, right, sometimes 7 days a week, right, depends on what needs to be done.
finding: Day-to-day CFM governance works through paired GE and Safran counterparts in near-daily contact.

speaker: Mohammad Ehteshami, Vice President of Additive Integration
quote: Yes. Not in the additive, they have their own technology development, but the additive part of the fuel nozzle was developed by GE.
finding: In answer to whether the JV partner contributes equally on technology: inside CFM each partner keeps its own technology lines.

speaker: David Leon Joyce, Chief Executive Officer, President and Vice Chairman of GE
role_at_time: President & CEO, GE Aviation; Vice Chairman of GE
quote: On that franchise on the CFM56 for the Airbus and Boeing airplane, almost 80% of CFMs have less than or equal to 1 shop visit. So this is a very strong, very robust long-term franchise for us. And it fuels our investments in the rest of this business
finding: The CFM56 aftermarket is GE's cash engine and funds its new-engine investment.

speaker: David Leon Joyce, Chief Executive Officer, President and Vice Chairman of GE
role_at_time: President & CEO, GE Aviation; Vice Chairman of GE
quote: We at one point in time didn't expect to be shipping any CFMs past 2019. And now we're into 2019 and into 2020 with the existing Classic CFMs, which is fine with us.
finding: Lets demand run the CFM56 tail: CFM56 production was extended beyond 2019 because the transition to LEAP was slower than planned.

speaker: David Leon Joyce, Vice Chair
quote: In 2020, our LEAP volume will reach approximately 2,200 engines per year.
finding: Plan before COVID and the MAX grounding: about 2,200 LEAPs in 2020. Output fell to 845 in 2021, and later targets (2,000 in 2023) were also missed.

speaker: David Leon Joyce, Vice Chair
quote: CFM is of huge importance to both GE and the aviation industry and securing this transition to LEAP and successfully executing on the ramp secures the future of this business. The partnership between GE and Safran continues to deliver for the companies as well as the industry.
finding: Ranks the CFM56-to-LEAP transition as GE Aviation's top priority and credits the Safran partnership.

speaker: David Leon Joyce, Vice Chair
quote: We're holding 58% win rate on the neos320s (sic) [320neo] family and a sole source on the 737 MAX and the COMAC C919, which is still in development. On the 320neo family, our airline customers are averaging 95% utilization, which is 8.4 points better than our competition.
finding: CFM's position across Airbus, Boeing and COMAC, sold to airlines on a utilisation gap against the GTF.

speaker: Jamie S. Miller, Senior VP & CFO
quote: Yes. So it's consistent with our view over the last year, which has been breakeven in 2021.
finding: In 2019 LEAP OE breakeven was dated 2021; it later moved to 2025 and then to 2026.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: And obviously, we share that exposure with our joint venture partner, Safran. I think they were talking the other day about a EUR 200 million exposure in the second quarter if things stay as they are and we probably have something in that same range
finding: The MAX grounding cost is split symmetrically between the JV partners; GE sizes its own hit from Safran's disclosure.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: And I'm not a big fan of laying off our performance issues on anybody, be it a supplier, be it a customer or anyone else.
finding: Refuses to blame suppliers or the partner for LEAP delivery shortfalls.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: Well, I think we share Boeing's commitment to dealing with the current reality and working thoughtfully and deliberately toward a safe return to service. I think for us, it's really put some modest cash flow pressures on us here in the short term
finding: Supports Boeing in public during the grounding and calls the cash hit modest ($200-300m in Q2 2019).

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: I think both we and our partners at Safran have talked about our interest and our ongoing dialogue with Boeing in this regard. Some of those discussions, we probably want to keep between partners and between the customer. But really, what we want to do is look at the long-term economics for GE.
finding: Decision rule for new airframe engines such as the NMA: pursued jointly through CFM, but GE judges each on its own long-term economics and requires it to be accretive.

speaker: Andrew Burris Obin, BofA Merrill Lynch, Research Division
quote: Free cash flow drag on Aviation, $400 million. What has gotten worse? And the number seems to be quite a bit higher than what Safran is saying.
finding: Investors benchmark GE's MAX cash hit against Safran's; Miller says GE's quarterly drag rises to $400m with the second-half LEAP ramp while the MAX is grounded.

speaker: David Leon Joyce, Chief Executive Officer, President and Vice Chairman of GE
role_at_time: President & CEO, GE Aviation; Vice Chairman of GE
quote: And finally, we anticipate a reduction in CapEx as we slow our services build-out of LEAP, consistent with the new reality of the MAX deliveries.
finding: Cuts LEAP MRO capex in step with MAX delivery reality: capacity follows the airframer's actual rate.

speaker: David Leon Joyce, Chief Executive Officer, President and Vice Chairman of GE
role_at_time: President & CEO, GE Aviation; Vice Chairman of GE
quote: Through our CFM partnership, we're working very closely with Boeing and our customers with the #1 goal to achieve the safe return to service. We have reached an agreement with Boeing on payment terms for our production deliveries in '20 and the engines delivered in '19 that are on parked aircraft
finding: During the MAX grounding, CFM negotiated payment terms with Boeing for engines on parked aircraft instead of halting deliveries.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: So I think this year, you're going to see us probably spend, call it, several hundred million dollars less in engineering overall as we adjust to this environment. But that said, we really want to protect -- ... We really want to protect the underlying future technology bets that have always defined GE Aviation
finding: After Boeing shelved the NMA (GE, Safran and Pratt & Whitney had all weighed offers), cuts 2020 engineering by several hundred million dollars but protects next-generation technology bets, which became RISE.

speaker: Carolina Dybeck Happe, Senior VP & CFO
quote: So of course, when we compare us and Safran, we don't have exactly the same portfolios, right? ... But I would say, if you just compare our assumptions on narrow bodies with there, they're pretty aligned, right?
finding: When the two partners' outlooks differ, GE explains it by portfolio mix and confirms the narrowbody (CFM) assumptions match.

speaker: Carolina Dybeck Happe, Senior VP & CFO
quote: because of the open network model that we have, basically customers can service the engines that at not only different facilities around the globe, but they can also decide to go GE Safran or third party.
finding: Customers can choose GE, Safran or third-party shops: the parents both cooperate and compete for shop visits.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: Steve, on the CMRs, it was a narrowbody-oriented contract that we trued up in the quarter. With respect to the second part of that question regarding Safran, we'll leave their reports to them.
finding: Will not speak for Safran's results, even on shared narrowbody contracts; each partner reports its own half.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: John Slattery, in concert with our partners at Safran, announced the CFM RISE program, which really is a multigenerational technology investment program ... to launch technologies that ultimately transition into product programs as our airframer and airline customers deem appropriate.
finding: RISE was launched jointly with Safran as a technology programme; the move to a product is left to the airframers' timing.

speaker: John Stephen Slattery, Senior Vice President
role_at_time: Senior Vice President (CEO of GE Aviation)
quote: Remember, we delivered 845 LEAPs last year. We expect to deliver and target to deliver 2,000 LEAPs next year.
finding: Committed to 2,000 LEAPs in 2023, cut to 1,700 by mid-2023; actual growth in 2023 was about 25%.

speaker: Olivier Andries, Safran SA
role_at_time: CEO of Safran (as introduced on the call)
quote: In the short term, we are focusing on ... executing the ramp-up, the new ramp-up of the LEAP on a trajectory to deliver more than 2,000 engines by 2023.
finding: Safran also committed to more than 2,000 LEAPs in 2023; the target was missed by both partners.

speaker: Kathy MacKenzie, President and CEO of Commercial Engine Operations
role_at_time: President and CEO of Commercial Engine Operations
quote: We have taken 40% of the cost of the LEAP out of the LEAP engine since 2016. And with ongoing actions, we will breakeven by 2025.
finding: LEAP OE breakeven moved from 2021 (2019 view) to 2025 (2022 view) to 'OE profitability in 2026' (2025 view).

speaker: Mohamed Ali
role_at_time: VP of Engineering (title not printed on the turn)
quote: And that then is going to happen by the middle of this decade. ... And we'll test that and do a fly demo on that also by the middle of this decade.
finding: In 2022 GE dated the RISE demo and fly demo to about 2025; by July 2025 the flight test was 'this decade' with Airbus.

speaker: Olivier Andries, Safran SA
role_at_time: CEO of Safran (as introduced on the call)
quote: On the long-term future, we have decided to launch a revolutionary engine technology program, RISE with the aim to bring to market a disruptive engine by 2035, which would bring 20% fuel burn efficiency versus the latest generation engine
finding: Safran's CEO states the joint RISE goal: a disruptive engine by 2035 with 20% better fuel burn, a decision taken by both partners.

speaker: Olivier Andries, Safran SA
role_at_time: CEO of Safran (as introduced on the call)
quote: One of my first action, as a newly appointed CEO of Safran, was to announce together with my partner John Slattery, the extension of our partnership up to 2050.
finding: Safran's CEO, on GE's stage, confirms the CFM partnership was extended to 2050, agreed CEO to CEO with GE Aviation's head.

speaker: Olivier Andries, Safran SA
role_at_time: CEO of Safran (as introduced on the call)
quote: CFM International is a unique partnership that has been created nearly 50 years ago between GE and Safran. Together, we brought market at the time, disruptive engine, the CFM56 that has become the most popular commercial engine in the world.
finding: Safran's leader frames CFM as a partnership that brings a disruptive engine to market once a generation.

speaker: Kathy MacKenzie, President and CEO of Commercial Engine Operations
role_at_time: President and CEO of Commercial Engine Operations
quote: We are so proud of the partnership we have had with Safran. The history on the CFM, the current product with LEAP and then our future and our focus on sustainable flight, we couldn't be more aligned.
finding: GE's engine-programmes chief says GE and Safran are fully aligned across CFM56, LEAP and RISE.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: At Aerospace, our joint venture with Safran. CFM International was selected by Delta to deliver 200 CFM LEAP-1B engines to power its new fleet of Boeing 737-10 aircraft, with options for up to 60 additional engines.
finding: CFM's MAX exposure includes the uncertified 737-10; large LEAP-1B orders tie CFM's ramp to Boeing's certification timing.

speaker: Carolina Dybeck Happe, Senior VP & CFO
quote: I don't want to speak for them specifically. I would say, overall, everyone is in this together, and it's very well aligned
finding: Asked whether GE or Safran is the bigger LEAP supply constraint, refuses to speak for the partner and presents the JV as aligned.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: What we've tried to do is avoid the finger pointing. We've tried to avoid the public posturing and just get to work, right?
finding: Refuses to blame a single supplier or the partner in public for LEAP shortfalls.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: LEAP is a platform where we've got 3 engines, 2 of them, the 1A for Airbus 1B for Boeing, basically have on the order of 2,500 parts each. ... they're only about 10% of those parts that are common across both platforms.
finding: The LEAP-1A and -1B share only ~10% of parts, so CFM runs two separate supply ramps for Airbus and Boeing.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: I would say that it's going to be a significant undertaking this year to see our LEAP volumes up 50%. Both GE and Safran are 2 partners of the CFM joint venture are committed to doing that. We've set as much to both our major airframer customers.
finding: LEAP rate commitments to Boeing and Airbus are made jointly by both JV partners; the 2023 +50% commitment was missed (+25%).

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: As it stands today, LEAP has a shortfall in time-on-wing, particularly in the Middle East and India. Sounds familiar? There are a small, handful of parts that are causing that.
finding: Admits the LEAP durability shortfall in hot-and-harsh regions and frames it as a fix to a few parts, as was done on the GE90.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: Now I always get that question, including last night, do we have to wait until RISE suite of technologies develop and all of them mature ... And the answer is no. We are actually working on upgrades.
finding: RISE technologies are fed back into LEAP upgrades, protecting the installed base while the next engine matures.

speaker: Russell T. Stokes, President and CEO of Commercial Engines & Services - GE Aerospace
role_at_time: President and CEO of Commercial Engines & Services
quote: As the LEAP comes into service and customers get familiar with the technology, we do see more CSA penetration than what we would see on CFM at this point in time. ... The CSAs, we tend to underwrite internally.
finding: Early LEAP risk sits on the JV parents' balance sheets through internally underwritten CSAs, unlike the open CFM56 model.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: And let me tell you, anybody who will tell you that they need to redesign a large portion of the engine in order to achieve the customer expectations, you should be worried. But that's not what we are doing.
finding: Implicit contrast with a rival's larger durability redesign: CFM's fix is incremental.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: Our external network for LEAP is now up to 5 partners, creating a highly competitive environment that drives a lower cost of ownership for our airline customers. Today, third-party MROs licensed by CFM service about 70% of the CFM56 shop visits.
finding: Copies the CFM56 licensed-network model (70% third-party) onto LEAP to lower cost of ownership and avoid tying up capital.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: For example, we're continuing our efforts to support the use of sustainable aviation fuel or SAF, the RISE program with CFM International. Our 50-50 JV with Safran aims to reduce fuel consumption and CO2 emissions by more than 20%
finding: Confirms that RISE sits inside the 50-50 CFM JV, so next-generation narrowbody propulsion stays a shared GE-Safran bet.

speaker: Russell T. Stokes, President and CEO of Commercial Engines & Services - GE Aerospace
role_at_time: President and CEO of Commercial Engines & Services
quote: All of these actions and activities, we believe lead us to a place where we see OE breakeven and program profitability by the middle of the decade.
finding: In 2023 LEAP OE breakeven was still promised for the middle of the decade; by 2025 OE profitability was dated 2026.

speaker: Russell T. Stokes, President and CEO of Commercial Engines & Services - GE Aerospace
role_at_time: President and CEO of Commercial Engines & Services
quote: We have held a sole-source position on some of the most amazing narrow-body platforms that this industry has seen in its history. And we've sustained that position on the MAX. We have a strong position on the A320. 55% of the NEOs have LEAP-1A engines under wing. And on the C-19, it's a LEAP-1C.
finding: Lays out CFM's three-airframer position: sole source on the MAX, ~55% of the neo fleet, and the LEAP-1C on COMAC's C919.

speaker: Mohamed Ali, Vice President of Engineering
quote: It's going to be nearly impossible for anybody to come from behind without that experience and without these hundreds of millions of cycles of experience in GE90 and GEnx and develop a high-pressure ratio machine that will work with a high time on wing and high durability in the hot and harsh environment.
finding: Argues that the hot-section experience behind LEAP is a moat that rivals cannot quickly match.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: Tom Levin, who is over here, runs CFM programs for us. So he's out talking with those partners, and he's the one that facilitates the signing of those deals.
finding: GE has its own CFM programmes leader who signs the branded MRO partner deals. The transcript attributes this answer to Culp.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: So specifically to the A220-500, I think we'll keep our comments private. We'll have that conversation with Guillaume and his team. But obviously, as we evolve our product portfolio, we want to be on all the critical platforms that matter in the decades ahead.

quote: when you hear us refer to profitable market share, that is both an external and an internal recognition that it can't be share for share's sake. ... we are not the low bid, right.
finding: Rejects buying share on price; he wants to win on value and accepts losing low-bid competitions.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: We have changed the way the folks in the field are compensated, transitioning them, if you will, from volume to margin.
finding: Uses incentive design (pay on margin, not volume) to enforce pricing discipline in the sales force.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: We certainly want to make sure we get into an A-rated range and stay there over time. We think that's in the best interest of our shareholders. ... we think we get back to a place where we're going to be able to pay a dividend very much in line with our peers.
finding: Sets an A-rating target as the capital-structure anchor and makes restoring the dividend conditional on reaching it.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: we really want to make sure that we set our best businesses up to play offense, both organically and inorganically. That starts with Aviation, includes Healthcare, Renewables. Power has to earn that right.
finding: Ranks Aviation first for growth investment; capital goes to the strongest franchises and the turnaround business must earn it.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: And the way I've always operated is that's an investment. That's an investment that you ought to vet like R&D ... a big capital expenditure, and you ought to track the returns on it accordingly.
finding: Treats restructuring spend as a capital investment to be vetted and tracked for returns, like R&D or capex.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: I've never been big on managing by ratios. I think you manage program by program, investment by investment. ... if you look at Aviation, we are at a place, given where we are with LEAP, where we can tune down a little bit. But if you look at all-in R&D ... we're going to be at 7.5% of sales this year
finding: Allocates R&D program by program rather than to a ratio target; he allows Aviation R&D to ease after LEAP development while keeping all-in spend about 7.5% of sales.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: the reason this has been just such a blue-chip franchise for GE for years is because we have continued to invest in technology, and that's why we lead. ... But make no mistake about it, we need to continue to invest in technology. It's the seed corn of our future. We're not going to give that up.
finding: Protects Aviation technology spending even while deleveraging; R&D is 'seed corn' and is not cut for short-term cash.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: You and I talked about how we characterize the headwinds that we see from an operating margin perspective in Aviation, right? As one generation turns down, another generation LEAP comes on. We're providing that.
finding: Increases disclosure of the LEAP-transition margin headwind in Aviation in response to investor feedback.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: And one thing that I'm not going to tell you is something you want to hear that I don't know. ... We'll tell you what we know, we'll tell you what we don't know and we'll give you our best shot. Doesn't mean we'll always be right, but at least you'll know what we're thinking
finding: States his guidance rule: specific where known, directional further out, and never saying what investors want to hear without knowing it.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: I've never been somebody that's going to sit back, wait for BCG or McKinsey, JPMorgan to send a report. I need to get out. I need to feel it. I need to see it. I need to smell it.
finding: Decides from first-hand observation in plants and with customers rather than from consultant or banker studies.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: I don't think it's so precise to be formula driven, right, at 2.6x you can't, at 2.4x you can, right. It's really -- we need to be in a different zone with respect to our leverage to be able to think practically about reinvesting inorganically.
finding: Uses leverage as a judgement zone, not a mechanical trigger, for when M&A becomes possible; he will not lock himself to a single number.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: You don't want to hurt the customer. But the moment you say, "We can't cut cost in a certain area," guess what? You can't cut cost. It's that Toyota mindset of continuous improvement.
finding: Refuses to put any cost area off limits (the customer is the only constraint), applying Toyota-style continuous improvement.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: when some of the big commercial airframe programs begin to fade, we don't want to let those engineers go, right? We want to make sure they're still on the team, doing great work, developing technology, be it for the military, a commercial customer, so that we have that capability and that IP.
finding: Keeps engineering capacity between commercial engine programmes by moving it to military and other work, so that capability is ready for the next launch.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: We're at a point in the narrow-body cycle, right, where it is probably time to bring down that inventory a bit, get ready for LEAP
finding: Uses GECAS, the captive lessor, to shed older narrowbody inventory and prepare for LEAP-powered fleets, linking leasing to the engine transition.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: we want to run the company with a higher cash balance, both at Industrial and in Capital. We think that's just saner, safer management of the business.
finding: Prefers excess liquidity and less reliance on short-term funding, a conservative balance-sheet posture.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: new technology to work. So it'll be a while before we can say that issue is resolved once and for all. But I think we're trying to be as, again, we're trying to embrace our reality. Wish it didn't happen, fixing it, tending to the customers as best we can.
finding: Treats early field failures of a new technology (the HA turbine blade) as part of innovating; he is open with customers and fixes in the field, without abandoning the product.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: if you have a general management title, you're really responsible for that P&L. Lots of people can help, but at the end of the day, you need to integrate, you need to make those resource allocation decisions. You need to keep the expectation bar high. You need to hire or fire well
finding: Pushes decision rights and accountability down to P&L general managers, including resource allocation and hiring and firing.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: But let me remind you, this is a game of inches every single day, and I want us to keep score together along the way. Our goals are aligned with yours. This year will be more about what we do than what we say.
finding: Signature 'game of inches' framing; he invites investors to keep score and stresses deeds over words.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: Last year, our 4 industrial businesses collectively yielded mid-single-digit cash on sales. ... All in, I have confidence that our industrial businesses in aggregate should yield cash on sales more than double last year's levels over the long term.
finding: Sets a long-term aspiration to more than double free-cash-flow margins from mid-single digits, without a date.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: we expect significant improvement in Industrial free cash flows in 2020 that will take us positive for that year, GE Capital net income to be breakeven by 2021 and significantly lower corporate costs by 2021.
finding: Makes dated multi-year commitments (positive FCF in 2020, GE Capital breakeven by 2021); by January 2020 the 2020 FCF guide was $2-4bn positive.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: we're going from $4.5 billion prior to the dispositions to a range of breakeven to a negative $2 billion.
finding: Guides 2019 Industrial FCF to breakeven to minus $2bn, a deliberately low bar; he raises it in July and October, and the year closes at plus $2.3bn.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: These are discretionary decisions, which we could have chosen not to make this year. But I think this is what constitutes a reset.
finding: Chooses to take near-term cash pain (restructuring, the supply-chain finance exit) in the reset year, deliberately accepting worse 2019 numbers for long-term repair.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: First, put customers at the center of everything that we do; second, manage for operational performance first; third, set fewer and more impactful priorities.
finding: Sets three operating principles: customer first, operations before reporting, and fewer priorities.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: You know as well as I do that 1 quarter is a data point, not a trend. The guidance we provided a month ago remains unchanged.
finding: Does not raise guidance on a strong quarter driven by timing, which keeps credibility in reserve.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: As we said on the outlook call, we have not planned for perfection, meaning we have built in general contingencies to cover potential shortfalls related to market and execution risks. However, the grounding of the Boeing 737 MAX was not included in our original planning and presents a new risk.
finding: Discloses at once that the MAX grounding sits outside his planning contingency and flags it as a new risk.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: Well, I think that we probably will refrain from trying to quantify the size of the contingency, just to keep it as a contingency, right? ... But we don't want to necessarily bring excuses forward. We want to deliver results.
finding: Keeps the guidance cushion unquantified to preserve flexibility and refuses to pre-announce excuses (here, MAX).

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: Well, I would say, Nigel, if we put a 3-year timetable on it, it would no longer be aspirational, right? It would be a mid-term outlook. ... So I think for today, we'll keep the aspirations aspirational.
finding: Keeps long-term aspirations deliberately undated so they are not mistaken for commitments.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: We have a strong partnership with Boeing. We are confident in the 737 MAX aircraft. We are working closely with Boeing through the recertification process. And while the planes are on the ground, we are conducting proactive scheduled maintenance on the engines. The timing of the MAX's return to service is uncertain
finding: Publicly backs Boeing and the aircraft, uses the grounding for proactive LEAP-1B engine maintenance, and declines to forecast a return-to-service date.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: With respect to the MAX, first, let me express our deepest condolences to the families and friends of all those lost in the tragic accidents in Indonesia and Ethiopia. The flying public's confidence in the safety of flight is the foundation of the aviation industry. And we all take that responsibility as paramount.
finding: Opens on safety and public confidence before financial impact when addressing the MAX accidents.

speaker: H. Lawrence Culp, Chairman & CEO
quote: we share that exposure with our joint venture partner, Safran. I think they were talking the other day about a EUR 200 million exposure in the second quarter if things stay as they are ... we probably have something in that same range as a headwind
